chief_complaint: deep open sacral sore showing bone in bedridden patient
hpi_details: A 29-year-old man with paraplegia after a T6 spinal cord injury has been bedbound and presents with a deep sacral sore with exposed bone that has progressively worsened over several weeks.
ideas: He thinks his tailbone rubbed raw because his wheelchair cushion wore thin and put too much pressure on his skin.
concerns: He is worried that seeing bone in the wound means an emergency hospital admission and major surgery, causing him to fall behind in his online degree.
expectations: He hopes to get specialized wound care dressings and a referral for home nursing visits so he can treat the sore at home.
pmh: T6 spinal cord injury with paraplegia
social_hx: Bedbound and dependent on caregivers for repositioning; non-smoker

clinical_knowledge.topic: Pressure Ulcer Stage IV evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pressure Ulcer Stage IV is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Pressure Ulcer Stage IV: Debridement, pressure off-loading, nutrition support, flap surgery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pressure Ulcer Stage IV.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing systemic infection, spreading cellulitis, or pelvic osteomyelitis and offering closure before infection control and a sustainable off-loading plan.
management_principles: Plan for Pressure Ulcer Stage IV: Debridement, pressure off-loading, nutrition support, flap surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient with paraplegia after a T6 spinal cord injury, bedbound and dependent on caregivers for repositioning, presenting with a deep sacral sore with exposed bone. HPI: prolonged pressure ischemia.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Pressure Ulcer Stage IV.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Pressure Ulcer Stage IV.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess fever, chills, spreading erythema, escalating pain, and systemic illness; obtain deep tissue or bone specimens during debridement when osteomyelitis is suspected and tailor antibiotics to clinical findings and cultures. Maintain pressure redistribution, moisture and continence management, and nutrition support. Consider flap closure only through a specialist team after infection control and a durable off-loading plan are in place.

must_ask.say: How often are you repositioned or do you shift your weight during the day?
How long has this sore been getting worse, and has bone become visible?
Have you had any fevers or chills recently?
How has your appetite and weight been lately?
Has this wound been treated or debrided before?

history.answer: My caregiver noticed a deep open sore on my tailbone that has gotten so deep you can actually see the bone.
I didn't suffer any cut or fall; it developed from lying on my back in bed for long hours without turning.
The skin started turning red about six weeks ago, and over the past three weeks it broke down rapidly into an open hole.
It is right over my sacrum and tailbone, and it looks like a wide, deep crater where the hard bone is completely exposed.
There has been yellowish fluid soaking through the pads every day, and my caregiver noticed a foul, rotten smell coming from it.
No, I haven't fallen, been bitten by an animal, or had any soil or foreign objects in the wound.
It oozes a little pinkish fluid when the bandages are changed, but there has never been any heavy or spurting bleeding.
I don't feel any pain or tenderness there because I have lost all sensation below my chest from my spinal cord injury.
My family has just been cleaning it with normal saline and covering it with dry gauze, without any prescription ointments or doctor visits.
No, I was never burned by hot water, fire, a heating pad, or any caustic chemicals.
No, I haven't been in any fires or smoky rooms, and I don't have a cough, hoarseness, or trouble breathing.
My family tries to turn me every few hours, but because of their work schedules, I often lie flat on my back for four to six hours at a time.
I haven't had any high fevers, chills, or night sweats, but I have felt more tired and run-down lately.
I have an indwelling urinary catheter, but bowel accidents occasionally soil the tailbone area before my caregiver can clean me up.
My appetite has been very poor recently, and I lost about five kilograms over the past two months because I only eat a few bites each meal.
Ever since my injury, I cannot move my legs at all and I have no sensation from my mid-chest downwards.
I do not have diabetes, high blood pressure, or any known circulation problems in my legs.
No, nothing like that at all. This sore is entirely from being bedbound and unable to move.
I had a tetanus booster shot three years ago when I had surgery for my spinal cord injury.
I have complete paraplegia from a T6 spinal cord injury caused by a car accident three years ago.
I had emergency spinal stabilization surgery and fusion three years ago right after the car crash.
I am not taking any prescription medications, steroids, or blood thinners.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink any alcohol.
I live at home with my elderly mother and a part-time caregiver, but lifting and repositioning me regularly has been very difficult for them.
There is no family history of chronic skin conditions, bleeding disorders, or poor wound healing.

I thought my skin just broke down because my wheelchair cushion wore out and pressed directly against my tailbone. I'm worried that having exposed bone means I'll be stuck in the hospital for major surgery and fail my college classes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Chronically ill-appearing, thin male resting in bed with an indwelling urinary catheter, oriented and in no acute respiratory distress.

Large 6 by 5 cm sacral ulcer with full-thickness tissue loss, central yellowish slough, exposed sacral bone with positive probe-to-bone test, surrounding 2 cm rim of erythema and warmth, and foul-smelling purulent discharge.
Bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric, with capillary refill under two seconds in all toes.
Normal sensation to light touch and pinprick from C2 to T5 dermatomes, with complete anesthesia to all sensory modalities below the T6 level including the perineum and lower extremities.
Upper extremity motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally; lower extremities demonstrate 0/5 flaccid paralysis bilaterally.
Biceps and triceps reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally with no Babinski sign.
Trace dependent bilateral ankle edema without calf tenderness or palpable venous cords.
